title: CS3301 Data Structures — Week 6: Python Recursion
description: Core concepts of recursion in Python: base cases, recursive steps, call stack frames, and return propagation.

style_descriptions.analogy: Real-world analogy grounding the abstract concept in familiar physical metaphors
style_descriptions.trace: Step-by-step state and execution trace showing variables and frames

quiz.text: What is the base case in factorial(n)?
What happens if countdown(n) has no base case?
Given def f(n): return n + f(n-1) with f(0)=0, what is f(3)?
In sum_list([3,1,4]), how many times is sum_list called in total?
At the deepest point of factorial(4), how many frames are on the stack?
What is the first frame removed from the stack during factorial(3)?
In factorial(3), what does factorial(1) return to factorial(2)?
In fib(4) (naive), what value does fib(2) return?

base_case.text: In def power(x, n): if n == 0: return 1; return x * power(x, n-1), what is the base case?

recursive_step.text: Given def multiply(a, b): if b == 0: return 0; return a + multiply(a, b-1), what is multiply(3, 4)?

call_stack.text: At the deepest point of power(2, 3) where power(x, n) calls power(x, n-1) with base case n == 0, how many frames are on the stack?

return_propagation.text: In power(2, 3), what does power(2, 1) return to power(2, 2)?

base_case.text: In def gcd(a, b): if b == 0: return a; return gcd(b, a % b), what is the base case?

recursive_step.text: Given def count_down(n): if n == 0: return 0; return 1 + count_down(n-1), what is count_down(5)?

call_stack.text: In sum_to(5) where sum_to(n) calls sum_to(n-1) with base case n == 0, how many frames are on the stack at the deepest point?

return_propagation.text: In sum_to(3), what does sum_to(1) return to sum_to(2)?
